accuracy.evidence: KS3 wording checked against the DfE English programme of study (2013): a wide range of fiction and non-fiction, whole books, short stories, poems and plays across genres, periods, forms and authors, pre-1914 and contemporary literature, two Shakespeare plays, seminal world literature, choosing books for challenge, interest and enjoyment. Dates: Romeo and Juliet written about 1595, first printed 1597 (Folger Shakespeare Library); Frankenstein published January 1818 (British Library); Anne Frank's diary written June 1942 to August 1944 (Anne Frank House); Noughts & Crosses 2001 (Penguin). Vocabulary thresholds of about 98% known words for unassisted reading and about 95% with effort from Hu & Nation (2000) and Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010); the lesson presents them as a rough guide, not a rule. Great Fire of London began in Pudding Lane in 1666 (Museum of London); Europa is a moon of Jupiter (NASA).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips about independent reading at this age: volume mistaken for breadth (log prediction, repeat-fantasy feedback 'more books, still 1 kind', p2, m4, tag many); avoiding any difficulty or abandoning stretch books (stretch prediction, bin feedback, m3, tag hard); memoir mistaken for fiction because it is a first-person story (genre sort, p5, tag memo); older texts dismissed or assumed to start as films (Frankenstein prediction, m6, tags time and old).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwide is built on reading breadth itself: a bar chart of a one-genre reading log whose 'kinds covered' count rises only when a new kind is added, pages that reveal their tricky-word count before being sorted into comfort / stretch / not yet, a four-century timeline for named texts, and a pages-per-day slider that colours a 28-day calendar. flagrecbk (matching readers and reasons), flagbkcmp (comparing two novels) and flaggenre (writing in forms) use none of these; the distinct gate passed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea comes from doing: dragging a second fantasy book raises the book count but leaves 'kinds covered: 1 of 7'; tapping a page shows 1, 3 or 9 tricky words in 50 before the learner decides; dropping the 9-word page in Stretch is told one word in five is too many to follow; the calendar turns green inside two weeks only when pages per day reach 18 or more for 240 pages.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options, each disproved by the next task: 'yes, 30 books is a lot' (the log shows one kind), 'yes, reading should never feel hard' (the stretch page is the one that grows you), and 'in the last 100 years, as a film story' for Frankenstein (the timeline places it in the 1800s, 1818).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions (widening a mysteries-only log, naming a sci-fi opening, a 3-in-50 page, the oldest text, days to finish 300 pages at 15 a day, memoir fiction or non-fiction, why read a 200-year-old novel). Wrong options carry tags many, genre, hard, time, math, memo and old, each with its own message naming the slip, e.g. 'Divide the pages by pages a day: 300 ÷ 15 = 20 days.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the learner limits (kid ≤ 6.5, adult ≤ 9.5). Kid paragraphs define genre, form and memoir before using them and keep sentences short ('Old books are worth it.'). The adult text gives KS3 terms (genre, form, convention, period, stamina) and states the vocabulary threshold as a guide with a caution.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: genre and form, wide versus many, why older books, comfort versus stretch and stamina. Adult: KS3 requirements, terms and the vocabulary-coverage evidence, four named mistakes with a caution, then exactly what the lab does. No filler pattern matched and the 12% duplicate gate passed against 481 Recommending Books, 487 Comparing Books and 518 Writing Across Genres.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android light and dark and iPhone-size screenshots after Show me on every step. Fixed from the first pass: the reading-log bar labels at 10 px collided with the 'kinds covered' line, now the chart is shorter, labels are 11 px short names and the count sits on its own line; 'The Diary of a Young Girl' was cut at three lines, now wraps to four with a shorter date. Real pointer drags (log books, pages into boxes, the slider) and page taps were tested at 390 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin: one per genre, '+ <title>' per shelf book, 'Check page A/B/C' then one button per box, one per century, and −1 / +1 page-a-day buttons. The canvas aria-label and live region carry every message, including the kinds count and days to finish. walk.cjs passed axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console or page errors.

sources: Department for Education (2013): English programmes of study, Key Stage 3 (reading)
Hu, M. & Nation, P. (2000). Unknown vocabulary density and reading comprehension. Reading in a Foreign Language 13(1)
Laufer, B. & Ravenhorst-Kalovski, G. C. (2010). Lexical threshold revisited. Reading in a Foreign Language 22(1)
Folger Shakespeare Library: Romeo and Juliet (date and first printing)
Anne Frank House: the diary (written 1942–1944, published 1947)
Museum of London: the Great Fire of London, 1666, Pudding Lane
